newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: No sudden upturn seen in European feed demand.
newsitem.headline: No sudden upturn seen in European feed demand.

text.p: European feed demand is not expected to pick up dramatically this week, despite last Friday's weaker Chicago futures close, traders said on Monday.

They said activity was likely to be muted given that markets will be closed on Friday ahead of the Easter weekend, the dollar is hovering around 1.70 marks and there is negative sentiment due to the confirmation of the Netherlands' first BSE case and the ongoing swine fever problem.
"High prices, especially in comparison to feed grains, will keep turnover down," one dealer said.
Soymeal prices in Europe have soared to around $80/tonne above last year's levels. In comparison Argentine sunmeal is still trading at around year-ago levels.
"As Chicago markets are being directed by the funds it is difficult to predict what will happen next, but a break in prices has to come sooner or later," one broker said.
Consumers have shied away from the soymeal market and only covered their immediate needs, picking up mid-protein material.

But soymeal is not completely replaceable and consumers are not fully covered for the summer months while physical soymeal will remain tight until supplies from South America arrive in Europe, possibly as late as June.

Swine fever in the Netherlands has prompted the slaughter of some 800,000 pigs in the past month, some five percent of the total Dutch pig population, and could theoretically reduce demand for pig feed by a similar percentage, making consumers wary of buying raw material, dealers said.

"Swine fever and BSE could have a sentimental negative impact on the market, just as cattle are due to go back out into the fields, which decreases nearby compound feed use by farmers. The question is, how negative," one dealer said.
